A Data-Driven Approach to Predicting Romantic
Relationship Outcomes Using Chat-Based

Sentiment Analysis: An Expanded Framework and
Ethical Analysis
Robin Rajesh
MSc Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
Christ (Deemed to be University), Bangalore, India

Email: robin.trajesh@gmail.com
Abstract—The digital era has revolutionized the way individ-
uals communicate and form relationships. Text messaging has
become the primary channel for romantic interaction, leaving
rich linguistic and emotional traces that can be leveraged for un-
derstanding relationship dynamics. This expanded paper explores
the potential of sentiment and behavioral analysis in predicting
romantic relationship breakups using chat data. A large-scale
dataset of 15,000 simulated chat exchanges was developed to
mimic realistic emotional and conversational patterns observed
during stable and deteriorating relationships. Using machine
learning and deep learning models, the study identifies linguistic
and emotional indicators that correlate strongly with declining
relationship health. Among the tested models, XGBoost achieved
the highest accuracy of 91%, outperforming classical baselines
and complex deep learning networks. The superior performance
of the XGBoost classifier validates the use of handcrafted,
sociolinguistic features derived from psychological constructs
(such as pronoun ratio and response delay) as highly effective
predictors for long-term relational forecasting. Results highlight
key predictive markers such as decreasing sentiment consistency,
increasing conflict-related expressions, and growing individual-
istic language usage. We also provide a comprehensive ethical
assessment and roadmap for multimodal system expansion.
Index Terms—Sentiment Analysis, Relationship Prediction,
Chat Analysis, NLP, Emotional Modeling, Behavioral Analytics,
Algorithmic Bias, Differential Privacy
I. INTRODUCTION ANDSTRATEGICOVERVIEW
A. Initial Context and Research Goals
Romantic relationships are central to emotional well-being,
yet many end abruptly due to gradual communication break-
downs that often go unnoticed. Recent advancements in Natu-
ral Language Processing (NLP) and affective computing offer
new opportunities to analyze digital interactions to detect
emotional distress and predict relational outcomes.[1, 2, 3]
Text-based communication captures intimate aspects of re-
lationship dynamics—tone, sentiment, response patterns, and
emotional volatility. By analyzing such data, one can uncover
meaningful trends that precede breakups, such as emotional
withdrawal, negative tone escalation, and reduced empathetic
expressions. The research confirms the potential to extract
structural, linguistic, and behavioral markers that indicate de-clining relational health, setting a precedent for non-invasive,
data-driven diagnostic tools.
B. Key Findings and Technical Validation
The core technical achievement of the study is the high
predictive accuracy demonstrated by the optimized XGBoost
classifier, which attained 91% accuracy on the binary classi-
fication task. This performance exceeded both classical statis-
tical models and state-of-the-art deep learning architectures,
specifically the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network
(89%) and the BERT-based fine-tuning model (90%).[4, 5]
This finding is crucial, suggesting that for the specific domain
of long-term relational forecasting, **handcrafted, sociolin-
guistic features** derived from psychological constructs are
superior predictors when combined with a robust ensemble
learning algorithm.[4]
II. RELATEDWORK
Several studies have investigated the relationship between
communication behavior and relationship satisfaction. Seraj
et al. (2021) demonstrated that linguistic patterns on social
media change markedly before breakups—showing more self-
referential language and negative emotion words weeks be-
fore separation.[4] Garimella et al. (2014) analyzed Twitter
exchanges and found that couples who eventually separated
displayed lower levels of positive interaction and mutual
engagement.[5]
Hutto and Gilbert (2014) introduced the V ADER model
for sentiment analysis of short texts, which remains a cor-
nerstone in emotional polarity scoring.[1] Zhang and Kim
(2022) later extended this work by using transformer-based
emotion detection models for conversational data.[7] Research
by Pennebaker (2011) on pronoun use revealed that higher
“I” usage correlates with detachment, whereas “we” usage
indicates mutual closeness.[1, 8] The present work extends
this field by constructing a diverse and balanced chat dataset
for controlled experimentation and predictive modeling.

III. DATASETCONSTRUCTION ANDPREPROCESSING
A. Dataset Overview
A large corpus of chat dialogues between hypothetical
couples was generated to emulate both stable and conflict-
prone interactions. This simulated approach addresses the pro-
found ethical and privacy constraints of accessing real intimate
conversation records.[9] Each record includes metadata such
as message time, sentiment score, response delay, and emotion
category.

TABLE I: Chat Dataset Statistics
Attribute Description

breakup)
Average Messages per Chat 65
Average Response Time 38 seconds
Average Word Count per
Message13.8

Negative Sentiment Ratio 0.24 (Stable), 0.56 (Breakup)
B. Preprocessing
Messages were tokenized, lowercased, and cleaned by re-
moving emojis and repeated characters. Linguistic features
such as pronoun ratios, negation frequency, and sentiment
polarity were computed. Stop words were removed, and emo-
tional intensity scores were normalized to the range .
IV. METHODOLOGY

The system pipeline consists of four primary stages: mes-
sage preprocessing, feature extraction, model training, and
prediction. Figure 1 illustrates the architecture of the overall
workflow.
Fig. 1: System Workflow for Relationship Breakup PredictionA. Feature Engineering
Features were derived from linguistic (L-Features) and
behavioral (B-Features) dimensions [10]:
•Sentiment Polarity:Using V ADER and TextBlob to
assign sentiment scores to each message.
•Emotional Variability:Measuring fluctuations in emo-
tional tone within a given chat, which reflects a failure
in physiological self-soothing.[11]
•Response Delay (τ):Capturing communication
gaps that reflect emotional distancing, a proxy for
Stonewalling.[12]
•Pronoun Distribution (P ratio):Evaluating ratio of “I”
to “we” to detect self-focus, a marker of psychological
withdrawal.[1, 13]
•Conflict Indicators:Keyword-based detection of argu-
mentative tone and negative emotional keywords, related
to Criticism and Contempt.[14]
B. Model Selection
Multiple classifiers were trained and compared, including
Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, LSTM, and a
BERT-based fine-tuned model for sequence classification. Grid
search optimization and 5-fold cross-validation were used to
fine-tune hyperparameters.
V. DETAILEDANALYSIS ANDPREDICTIVELANDSCAPE
A. Theoretical Anchors: Gottman’s Framework in Text
The data generation protocol leveraged Dr. John
Gottman’s framework of the ”Four Horsemen of the
Apocalypse”—Criticism, Contempt, Defensiveness, and
Stonewalling—as reliable predictors of dissatisfaction.[15]
The feature importance analysis revealed that ”Trust-related
Keywords” and conflict indicators held the highest predictive
value (22% importance), acting as robust proxies for
Criticism and Contempt.[14] Similarly, the high importance
of Emotional Variability (17%) indicates a failure in emotional
regulation, which is the systemic failure corresponding to
Stonewalling.[11]
B. Linguistic Markers of Detachment
The study validated the application of quantitative sociolin-
guistics by Pennebaker.[6] The Pronoun Distribution Ratio
(Pratio), which measures the shift from ”we” to ”I” usage,
emerged as the second most important predictive feature (18%
importance). This high ranking confirms that self-focus signals
psychological withdrawal and detachment from the shared
relational unit.[1, 8]
C. Digital Trace: Behavioral Signals
The Average Response Delay (τ) was utilized as a func-
tional proxy for Stonewalling. Its substantial importance
(14%) confirms that timing is a potent indicator of relational
health.[16] The time-series analysis showed that increased
message delay and reduced positive tone were strong indi-
cators of relationship distress, though the relational impact of

delayed responses is context-sensitive (e.g., more critical in
long-distance relationships).[16]
VI. MODELPERFORMANCE ANDFEATUREIMPORTANCE
A. Model Comparison
Table II presents the comparison of all models.

TABLE II: Model Performance Comparison
Model Accuracy Precision Recall F1-Score
Logistic Regression 0.80 0.78 0.79 0.78
Random Forest 0.86 0.84 0.85 0.84
LSTM 0.89 0.88 0.89 0.88
BERT 0.90 0.89 0.90 0.89
XGBoost 0.91 0.90 0.91 0.90
The XGBoost model achieved the highest performance
across all metrics. The marginal performance gap between
XGBoost (91%) and BERT (90%) dictates a preference for
the former, as XGBoost provides explicit feature importance
scores, prioritizing interpretability over marginal black-box
accuracy for sensitive behavioral health applications.[5]
B. Feature Importance
Fig. 2: Feature Importance derived from XGBoost Model
Key predictors included trust-related keywords (22%), pro-
noun ratio (18%), and emotional variability (17%). Increased
message delay and reduced positive tone were also strong
indicators of relationship distress.C. Sentiment Dynamics
Fig. 3: Average Sentiment Trend over Time for Stable vs.
Breakup Conversations
Figure 3 shows a clear divergence: stable conversations
maintained balanced emotional trajectories, contrasting with
breakup-labeled conversations, which showed a noticeable
downward trend in sentiment consistency. The high impor-
tance of sentiment *variability* (17%) relative to the *mean*
negative sentiment (9%) suggests that emotional stability and
predictability are more fundamental determinants of relation-
ship health than overall negative tone.
VII. ETHICALCONSIDERATIONS ANDFUTUREWORK
A. Ethical Constraints of Synthetic Data
The reliance on synthetic data, while necessary for training
and validating ML algorithms under controlled conditions [9],
introduces challenges in external validity. For a predictive
model to be generalizable, the synthetic data must be rigor-
ously evaluated against metrics such as Fidelity, Diversity, and
Generalization.[6, 17]
Moving toward ethical deployment mandates privacy stan-
dards. Should the system integrate real data, the implementa-
tion of Differential Privacy (DP) using DP-SGD (Differentially
Private Stochastic Gradient Descent) is mandatory to prevent
the model from leaking sensitive information.[18] Privacy
must also be assessed using quantitative metrics such as
Identifiability Scores (IS) and Membership Inference Attacks
(MIAs) to ensure the generated data is ”different enough” from
original records.[19]
B. Algorithmic Bias and Fairness Audits
AI models trained on sociolinguistic data are highly sus-
ceptible to inheriting and amplifying societal biases.[20] A
significant risk is **heteronormative bias**, where models

may prefer or provide inequitable results for non-traditional
relationships.[21, 22] Furthermore, the model must guard
against gendered bias, ensuring features are assessed con-
sistently regardless of which partner expresses them.[23] To
ensure fairness, the framework requires explicit algorithmic
auditing using adapted challenge datasets (like CrowS-pairs)
and sociolinguistic countermeasures to debias the language
models.[13]
C. Multimodal System Expansion
To advance the predictive power, future research must
expand the feature set to integrate sophisticated multimodal
cues:
•Dedicated Emoji Analysis:Emojis are crucial, often
non-verbal, emotional cues.[24, 25] Future feature ex-
pansion must incorporate specific emoji embeddings and
utilize **multimodal fusion** where the symbolic mean-
ing and visual semantics of emojis are blended with the
semantic representations of the text features, allowing the
model to capture nuances like irony or sarcasm.[24, 26]
•Micro-Temporal Cues:Beyond aggregated response
delay, analysis of micro-temporal patterns (e.g., typing
and editing speed) can provide richer behavioral signals
indicative of internal conflict or distress.[27]
Integrating these features will necessitate a transition toward
hybrid deep learning frameworks optimized for multimodal
emotion recognition, employing CNNs for spatial features,
RNNs/LSTMs for temporal dynamics, and Transformer atten-
tion mechanisms for robust multimodal fusion.[28, 29]
VIII. CONCLUSION ANDSTRATEGICRECOMMENDATIONS
This research demonstrates the feasibility of predicting
romantic relationship breakups using sentiment and behavioral
analysis of chat messages. By employing advanced NLP and
machine learning methods, emotional and linguistic signals
that precede relationship dissolution were successfully identi-
fied. XGBoost achieved the highest predictive accuracy (91%),
followed closely by transformer-based models.
The findings indicate that the erosion of trust (Conflict
Keywords) and psychological detachment (P ratio) are the
core predictive drivers, confirming the strong link between
computational sociolinguistics and clinical relationship theory.
The superior performance of XGBoost validates the efficacy
of theory-driven, handcrafted features in this domain.[4]
Future research must prioritize interpretability, ensuring the
system provides actionable, risk-focused guidance rather than
declarative predictions (mitigating the risk of self-fulfilling
prophecy), and continue the expansion into multimodal anal-
ysis with strict ethical guardrails regarding privacy and bias.

ALL SERVICES ARE PROVIDED "AS IS" AND "AS AVAILABLE" WITH ALL FAULTS. 14.
